planting.note: Lightly scarify the hard seed coat and sow in fall for natural winter stratification into a lean, gritty scree in full sun; established cushions can also be moved as small divisions in spring.

directions: Dwarf Alpine Clover hugs the ground in tight mats of tiny gray-green trifoliate leaves, almost disappearing into the gravel except when its oversized pink-purple pea flowers open directly at the cushion surface in early summer. It colonizes exposed fellfields and wind-scoured ridgetop turf above treeline across the central and southern Rocky Mountains, rooting into fine scree where competing vegetation cannot establish. Grow in a lean, sharply drained scree bed or trough in full sun, keeping it on the dry side; it is a true miniature even among alpines, rarely exceeding the thickness of the gravel it grows in. Humid, rich, or poorly drained sites quickly cause the taproot to rot.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall and let winter cold break dormancy, planting into a gritty, humus-poor scree mix; it tolerates slightly more moisture at the root than many fellfield alpines but still demands sharp drainage.

directions: This diminutive harebell produces a single nodding, deep violet-blue bell on a thread-thin stem barely taller than the surrounding rock and gravel, rising from a sparse tuft of small basal leaves. It is primarily a circumpolar Arctic and Beringian specialist, but genuine disjunct populations reach high alpine tundra in British Columbia, Utah, and Colorado, where it grows in rocky turf, scree margins, and gravelly ridges well above treeline. Grow in a gritty, sharply drained scree or trough in full sun with a cool root run; it is short-lived in cultivation but self-sows readily in congenial conditions. Avoid shade and rich garden soil, both of which cause it to grow soft and disappear.

planting.note: Sow in fall for winter stratification directly into a deep, loose scree or talus bed in full sun; the long taproot resents transplanting once established.

directions: Sky Pilot forms a mound of finely divided, sticky-glandular leaves with a distinctive skunky scent, topped from early to midsummer by dense clusters of funnel-shaped blue to lavender flowers with a contrasting orange-yellow throat. It is a summit specialist of loose talus, scree, and fellfield across the central and southern Rocky Mountains, often found at or near the highest rocky points a trail reaches. Plant into a deep, mineral, fast-draining scree in full sun so the taproot can run; it resents rich soil, summer humidity, and root disturbance. The pungent foliage scent is strongest when the leaves are brushed or crushed, a useful field character for distinguishing it from other alpine Polemonium.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring and plant into gritty, moisture-retentive scree near seep rock or talus; seed can also be fall-sown for spring germination but is slower to reach flowering size.

directions: King's Crown sends up thick, succulent, blue-green rosettes from a stout rootstock, crowned in early-to-mid summer by a tight dome of small dark red to maroon-purple flowers that give the plant its common name. It grows in rocky, often seep-fed talus, cliff ledges, and streamside scree near and above treeline throughout the Rocky Mountains and other high western ranges, tolerating more moisture at the root than most true fellfield alpines. Grow in a gritty but not bone-dry scree bed in full sun, ideally with a cool, slightly moist root zone emulating snowmelt seepage. It is one of the more forgiving alpine succulents in cultivation, closely related to the roseroot grown for its ornamental and traditional medicinal use.

planting.note: Sow in early spring into gritty, humus-rich crevice soil near rock seepage; it tolerates more shade and moisture than most alpine tundra plants and can also be started indoors and transplanted.

directions: Mountain Sorrel forms a low clump of rounded, kidney-shaped, fleshy leaves with a sharp, lemony tartness from oxalic acid, used by Arctic and alpine foragers as a vitamin C-rich wild green long before other plants are available. It grows tucked into cool, shaded rock crevices, talus, and seepy ledges from the circumpolar Arctic south through the alpine zone of the Rocky Mountains and other western ranges, favoring north-facing or shaded niches rather than open fellfield. In the garden, plant in a gritty crevice or shaded scree with reliable moisture at the root; it is far more shade- and moisture-tolerant than typical sun-loving alpines and makes an easy, edible rock-garden subject by comparison. Harvest young leaves for salads or as a sorrel substitute, same as its relative Rumex.

planting.note: Sow in fall for winter stratification into a deep, gritty scree or fellfield mix in full sun; plants are monocarpic, taking several years to build a large taproot and rosette before flowering once and dying.

directions: Old-Man-of-the-Mountain builds a dense rosette of silvery, hairy, finely divided leaves for several years before sending up a single oversized yellow sunflower-like head on a short stalk, famous for consistently facing east toward the rising sun. It is a signature plant of exposed, wind-blasted alpine tundra and fellfield in Colorado, Wyoming, and Montana, often the showiest bloom on an otherwise low, gray landscape above treeline; it is also known in botanical literature under the older name Hymenoxys grandiflora. It is monocarpic, flowering only once after accumulating enough reserves in its long taproot, then dying, so a planting needs a cohort of different ages to bloom in successive years. Grow in a deep, lean, sharply drained scree in full sun; it is slow from seed and rarely offered commercially, mostly grown from regional seed exchanges.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall and expose to a full winter freeze-thaw cycle, as germination is erratic without cold stratification; plant into humus-rich, moisture-retentive gritty soil rather than dry scree.

directions: Arctic Gentian produces short stems topped with upward-facing, creamy white to pale greenish-yellow flowers heavily streaked and spotted with purple inside, opening in the last weeks of the short alpine summer when most other tundra wildflowers have already finished. It grows in moist alpine turf, wet meadow margins, and grassy tundra swales near snowmelt across the Rocky Mountains of Colorado, Montana, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming and the circumboreal Arctic, needing more sustained moisture than scree-dwelling cushion alpines. Grow in a gritty but humus-enriched alpine bed that stays evenly moist through summer, in full sun with cool nights; it resents both drought and stagnant wet feet. Its very late bloom time makes it a prized, distinctive addition to a cool-climate alpine garden.

planting.note: Sow in fall for winter stratification, or plant small divisions in spring into gritty, slightly acidic alpine turf soil; it spreads slowly by short rhizomes once established.

directions: Creeping Sibbaldia spreads into a low mat of small, wedge-shaped, three-toothed leaflets resembling a miniature strawberry relative, with inconspicuous small yellow flowers opening close to the foliage in early summer. It carpets damp alpine turf, snowbed margins, and gravelly tundra meadows across the circumboreal north and the high Rocky Mountains, often among the first plants to green up as late snowbanks recede. Grow in gritty, humus-flecked alpine turf soil that stays cool and evenly moist, in full sun; it is a useful, low-key groundcover alpine for filling gaps between showier cushion plants in a trough or raised bed. It is more tolerant of routine garden moisture than true scree specialists, making it an easier entry point into alpine turf species.

planting.note: Sow in spring or plant divisions into a lean, sharply drained scree bed in full sun; established clumps can also be divided to increase stock.

directions: Alpine Sagebrush forms a low, spreading mat of finely divided, silvery, aromatic foliage with the familiar sage scent of its lowland sagebrush relatives, bearing small inconspicuous flower heads on short stalks in summer. Unlike big sagebrush of the dry steppe below, this dwarf alpine form grows in exposed fellfields and rocky alpine tundra ridges throughout the central Rocky Mountains, essentially restricted to Colorado, Wyoming, Utah, and Montana, hugging the ground to avoid constant wind. Grow in a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree in full sun; it is valued in alpine gardens chiefly for its silver foliage texture and tolerance of harsh, exposed sites rather than for showy bloom. It combines well with cushion-forming alpine flowers as a textural foil.

planting.note: Sow in fall for winter stratification into a lean, gritty scree or trough mix in full sun; small nursery-grown cushions can also be planted in spring.

directions: Alpine Sandwort builds dense, hard cushions of tiny needle-like leaves studded in summer with small white five-petaled flowers held just above the foliage, forming one of the classic fellfield cushion plants of the Rocky Mountain tundra; it is also known in some botanical treatments under the genus name Cherleria. It colonizes the most exposed, wind-scoured gravel ridges and rocky turf above treeline from the Sierra Nevada through the Colorado Rockies to Alaska, often alongside moss campion and other cushion specialists in the harshest available ground. Grow in a lean, mineral, sharply drained scree, crevice, or trough in full sun, keeping it dry at the crown; it is a favorite subject for alpine trough and container culture among rock garden enthusiasts. Rich soil, shade, or summer humidity will quickly weaken and rot the cushion.
